messages.content:
Rate the following clinical vignette:

He is 22, a South Eastern Asian man who now spends most of his days in front of a screen, adjusting spacing, color, and flow so that other people can move through an app without friction. Before the disaster, he likes that kind of work for the same reason he likes sketching interfaces in the margins of his notebooks: good design makes the world feel predictable. Buttons go where they should. Paths are clear. Things respond when touched. He is in university then, building a portfolio for UX jobs, freelancing a little, living with his parents and younger sister in a coastal city where the weather is usually something to be worked around, not feared.

The storm begins as inconvenience. Warnings come through phones and television, but storms are seasonal, familiar. He helps tape windows, move electronics higher, fill bottles with water. He remembers feeling mildly irritated that the power cuts out before he can save a design file. Even as the wind grows louder, he is still thinking in practical steps-charge devices, keep documents dry, check on neighbors. Then the water comes faster than anyone expects.

He remembers the sound first: not rain, but a heavy, advancing crash, as if the street itself has broken open. Water pushes through the lower level of the house with a force he has never imagined. Furniture lifts and turns. His mother is shouting for his sister. The lights are already gone, and in the dark he feels his way along a wall slick with water, calling out over the noise. For a moment he cannot find his father and is sure, with a cold certainty he still feels in his body when he talks about it, that he has lost him. They make it to the roof with a few neighbors, soaked and shaking, carrying almost nothing. He spends the night pressed between his family and strangers, listening to people pray, cry, and call names into the blackness. From that roof he sees parts of his neighborhood disappear.

In the days after, there is mud everywhere, the smell of fuel and sewage, the flat stunned look on faces he knows well. Their house is damaged beyond quick repair. A neighbor's body is found two streets away. Another family is still missing someone. He helps with cleanup because everyone helps. He carries debris, sorts ruined clothes, charges phones from a communal generator, and tries to act useful. People praise him for being calm. He clings to that version of himself. Inside, though, he is replaying the night in fragments-the slam of water against the door, his sister's voice, the brief instant when he cannot find his father. Each replay arrives as if it is happening again, not as memory but as a fresh jolt.

Months later, when the family relocates inland to stay with relatives, he tells himself he should be grateful. They are alive. He goes back to classes remotely, then later takes contract work as a UX designer. On the screen he can still make clean systems, but outside of work he begins organizing his life around threat. He checks weather apps compulsively, not just in the morning but every hour, zooming in on cloud bands and rainfall maps. If rain starts unexpectedly, his chest tightens so quickly he feels embarrassed by it. He scans exits in every building. He keeps his laptop and important documents packed in a waterproof bag by the door. At night he sleeps lightly, if at all, waking to the smallest sound with his heart racing. Sometimes he is back on the roof before he is fully awake, tasting dirty water, hearing people scream.

He avoids his old neighborhood altogether. Friends invite him to visit when they are back in the city, but he always has a reason not to go. He mutes group chats when people share storm footage. During monsoon season he becomes irritable and withdrawn. His mother notices he snaps at her when she leaves shoes near the door or forgets where the flashlights are. He hates himself afterward. He knows she survived the same night. Still, some part of him feels solely responsible for making sure it never happens again.

At work he is considered talented and exacting. He can spend an hour debating the safest, most intuitive path through a checkout screen, yet freeze if a coworker suggests an offsite meeting during heavy rain. In video calls, if someone's microphone picks up thunder, he loses the thread of conversation entirely. He says "sorry, bad connection," when really it is his mind that has gone elsewhere. He has become quieter with colleagues, reluctant to explain why he never joins beach outings or weekend trips near the water. Being single feels easier than trying to make anyone understand why he needs to know evacuation routes wherever he goes.

He speaks about the disaster with a flatness that breaks only in small moments-when he describes his sister shivering on the roof, or the shame he feels when he catches himself resenting ordinary rain. He says he used to think of himself as flexible, creative, someone who could improve messy systems. Now he feels brittle. The world that once seemed navigable feels unstable, and his body behaves as if catastrophe is not in the past but waiting just outside the frame.

These sentences explicitly show specific external cues (rain, thunder) that reliably activate distress and re-experiencing.
